questions.stem: A 50 year old man has noticed his rings and shoes no longer fit and his face has coarsened. He keeps bumping into people on both sides. Perimetry shows a bitemporal hemianopia that is denser in the upper quadrants.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his field defect?
questions.e: Upper quadrant defects worse than lower suggest inferior chiasmal compression, commonly a pituitary tumour; here a GH-secreting adenoma (acromegaly).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his field defect?

clues: rings and shoes no longer fit
steps.x: Bitemporal loss = chiasm; upper worse than lower = pressure from below, i.e. the pituitary.

elim: Craniopharyngioma compresses the chiasm from above, causing a defect worse in the lower quadrants.
Occipital lesions cause a homonymous hemianopia, not bitemporal loss.
MS typically causes monocular loss from optic neuritis.
A temporal lesion causes a contralateral superior quadrantanopia.

steps.x: Answer D: Pituitary adenoma. Bitemporal, upper > lower = inferior chiasmal compression, pituitary adenoma.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has 6 months of headaches and passes large volumes of dilute urine day and night. Perimetry shows a bitemporal hemianopia that is denser in the lower quadrants.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of compression of the optic chiasm?
o: From within the right optic nerve
questions.e: Lower quadrant defects worse than upper indicate superior chiasmal compression, commonly a craniopharyngioma, which is associated with diabetes insipidus.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely site of compression of the optic chiasm?
Lower field loss first means the upper chiasmal fibres are pressed, from above; DI suggests a craniopharyngioma.

elim: Compression from below (pituitary adenoma) affects the upper quadrants first.
A tract lesion causes a homonymous hemianopia.
Occipital lesions cause homonymous defects with macular sparing.
An optic nerve lesion causes monocular loss.

steps.x: Answer A: From above the chiasm. Bitemporal, lower > upper = superior compression (craniopharyngioma, with DI).

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has a glioma involving his left optic tract seen on MRI. He has a mild right-sided weakness. His visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely visual field defect?
questions.e: An optic tract lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, on the same side as any paresis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely visual field defect?
Behind the chiasm the left tract carries the right half of the visual field from both eyes.

elim: This results from a chiasmal lesion.
A left tract lesion affects the right visual field of both eyes.
Monocular loss comes from an optic nerve lesion.
This comes from a left temporal (Meyer's loop) lesion.

steps.x: Answer D: Right homonymous hemianopia. Optic tract lesion = contralateral homonymous hemianopia, same side as the paresis.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has had temporal lobe seizures for a year. Perimetry shows loss of the upper right quadrant of the visual field in both eyes. Visual acuity and fundoscopy are normal. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?
questions.e: A temporal lobe lesion causes a contralateral superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?

clues: upper right quadrant of the visual field in both eyes
steps.x: Upper quadrant = temporal (Meyer's loop); right field = left hemisphere.

elim: A left parietal lesion causes a right inferior quadrantanopia.
A chiasmal lesion causes a bitemporal hemianopia.
This causes a left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
A right temporal lesion causes a left superior quadrantanopia.

steps.x: Answer B: Left temporal lobe. Pie in the sky = contralateral temporal lobe.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man had a stroke 1 month ago. He now trips on kerbs and misses steps below him on the left. Perimetry shows loss of the lower left quadrant in both eyes. He also has left-sided neglect. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 142/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?
questions.e: A parietal lobe lesion causes a contralateral inferior quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor'); neglect also points to the right parietal lobe.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?

clues: lower left quadrant in both eyes
steps.x: Lower quadrant = parietal; left field = right hemisphere.

elim: A left parietal lesion causes a right inferior quadrantanopia.
Chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal loss.
An optic nerve lesion causes monocular loss.
A right temporal lesion causes a left superior quadrantanopia.

steps.x: Answer D: Right parietal lobe. Pie on the floor = contralateral parietal lobe.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has 4 days of blurred vision in her right eye with pain on eye movement. Colour vision is reduced in the right eye. There is a right relative afferent pupillary defect. The left eye and its visual field are normal. A year ago she had numbness of her legs that resolved.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?
questions.e: An optic nerve (pre-chiasmal) lesion, such as optic neuritis, causes monocular vision loss; the past sensory episode suggests multiple sclerosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?

clues: blurred vision in her right eye
left eye and its visual field are normal
steps.x: Only one eye affected with an RAPD = lesion in front of the chiasm.

elim: Occipital lesions cause homonymous defects in both eyes.
A tract lesion causes a right homonymous hemianopia in both eyes.
Chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal loss in both eyes.
This causes a left superior quadrantanopia in both eyes.

steps.x: Answer D: Right optic nerve. Monocular loss = optic nerve lesion (e.g. optic neuritis).

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped her apixaban a month ago. Yesterday she suddenly noticed she could not see things on her left. She has no limb weakness or speech problem. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye. CT head shows a right posterior cerebral artery territory infarct.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on formal perimetry?
o: Left homonymous hemianopia involving the macula
Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
questions.e: An occipital lobe lesion gives a homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, because the macular region has a dual blood supply.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on formal perimetry?

clues: right posterior cerebral artery territory infarct
Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye
steps.x: PCA infarct = occipital cortex; central (macular) vision is kept, so acuity is normal.

elim: This results from a chiasmal lesion.
Occipital infarcts typically spare the macula because of its dual blood supply.
This results from a right parietal lesion.
Monocular loss results from an optic nerve or retinal lesion.

steps.x: Answer C: Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Occipital lesion = homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has had a sudden loss of the right half of his vision in both eyes for 90 minutes, with unsteadiness and slurred speech. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm irregular, BP 176/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden-onset homonymous hemianopia raises concern for a posterior circulation stroke, which is an emergency.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: sudden loss of the right half of his vision in both eyes
steps.x: Sudden homonymous loss with brainstem/cerebellar symptoms and AF = posterior circulation stroke.

elim: Migraine aura is a positive, spreading visual disturbance that resolves within an hour, usually with headache.
Optic neuritis is monocular and painful.
Apoplexy gives sudden headache with bitemporal loss and ophthalmoplegia.
Detachment is monocular, with flashes and floaters.

steps.x: Answer D: Posterior circulation ischaemic stroke. Sudden homonymous hemianopia = posterior circulation stroke until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has been bumping into door frames on both sides and has had two near misses at junctions. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye. Confrontation testing shows loss of the outer half of the visual field in each eye. Fundoscopy is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?
questions.e: The pattern of field loss localises the lesion; loss of both temporal fields (bitemporal hemianopia) localises to the optic chiasm.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?

clues: bumping into door frames on both sides
loss of the outer half of the visual field in each eye
steps.x: Outer half of each eye's field = temporal fields; both lost = bitemporal hemianopia.

elim: A tract lesion causes a homonymous hemianopia.
Occipital lesions cause homonymous defects with macular sparing.
An optic nerve lesion causes monocular loss.
A temporal lesion causes a contralateral superior quadrantanopia.

steps.x: Answer C: Optic chiasm. Bitemporal hemianopia localises to the optic chiasm.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a bitemporal hemianopia from a 3 cm non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma. He declines treatment and misses follow-up for 2 years. He returns with much worse vision and pale optic discs on fundoscopy. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely consequence of the delay?
o: Complete recovery of vision without treatment
Development of a homonymous hemianopia only
questions.e: Visual field defects can cause permanent vision loss depending on the cause and speed of treatment; pale discs indicate optic atrophy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely consequence of the delay?

clues: much worse vision and pale optic discs
steps.x: Untreated chiasmal compression for years leads to optic atrophy.

elim: Prolonged compression causes optic atrophy, which does not recover.
Chiasmal compression does not convert to a homonymous defect.
This is unrelated to his tumour.
Pale discs mean optic atrophy, not papilloedema.

steps.x: Answer E: Permanent loss of vision. Untreated field defects risk permanent vision loss.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman had a right occipital stroke 3 months ago. Since then she has stopped reading the newspaper, has fallen twice at home and no longer goes out alone. Confrontation testing shows a left homonymous hemianopia. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. Cognitive testing is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her change in function?
o: Reduced quality of life from her visual field defect
questions.e: Visual field defects reduce quality of life: falls, difficulty reading and loss of independence.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for her change in function?
She cannot see her left side, so she falls and stops reading and going out.

elim: Cognitive testing is normal.
Cataract reduces acuity in each eye, not half the field of both eyes.
Her field defect directly explains the falls and loss of reading.
This causes dizziness on standing, not loss of half the visual field.

steps.x: Answer E: Reduced quality of life from her visual field defect. Field defects reduce quality of life (falls, reading, independence).

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has 5 days of painful loss of central vision in her left eye. Two years ago she had an episode of double vision that settled over a month. She has brisk reflexes in both legs. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her visual loss?
questions.e: Causes of visual field defects include stroke, tumour and multiple sclerosis; painful monocular loss in a young woman with previous episodes is optic neuritis from MS.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her visual loss?

clues: painful loss of central vision in her left eye
steps.x: Young, separate neurological episodes, UMN signs and painful monocular loss.

elim: GCA affects people over 50 and causes painless sudden loss.
A pituitary tumour causes bitemporal loss, not painful monocular loss.
Stroke causes homonymous loss in both eyes.
This is painless and usually in older people with vascular risk factors.

steps.x: Answer B: Multiple sclerosis. Young patient + optic neuritis + previous episodes = MS.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has 4 months of headaches, galactorrhoea and missed periods. She has noticed she clips wing mirrors on both sides when driving. MRI shows a pituitary macroadenoma extending upwards into the optic chiasm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely visual field defect?
o: Bitemporal hemianopia, worse in the lower quadrants
Bitemporal hemianopia, worse in the upper quadrants
questions.e: A pituitary adenoma compresses the chiasm from below, causing bitemporal hemianopia that starts in the upper quadrants.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely visual field defect?

clues: clips wing mirrors on both sides
extending upwards into the optic chiasm
steps.x: Pressure from below hits the inferior nasal crossing fibres first, which serve the upper temporal fields.

elim: Lower quadrants first suggests compression from above, e.g. craniopharyngioma.
This is an optic nerve lesion.
This results from a lesion behind the chiasm.
This results from a left temporal lesion.

steps.x: Answer B: Bitemporal hemianopia, worse in the upper quadrants. Pituitary adenoma: bitemporal hemianopia, upper quadrants first.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man attends the emergency department because he keeps knocking his right arm on door frames. He has no limb weakness. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 150/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Visual acuity is 6/9 in both eyes.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial assessment of his visual fields?
questions.e: Bedside confrontation testing is the initial assessment of a suspected visual field defect, followed by formal perimetry.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial assessment of his visual fields?

clues: keeps knocking his right arm on door frames
Visual acuity is 6/9 in both eyes
steps.x: Normal acuity but missing one side suggests a field defect; start at the bedside.

elim: This assesses retinal function and is not an initial field test.
This images retinal vessels, not the visual fields.
OCT images the retina and optic nerve head, not the fields.
These assess conduction in the optic pathway, not the shape of a defect.

steps.x: Answer A: Bedside confrontation testing. First assessment of a field defect = confrontation testing.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman had trans-sphenoidal surgery for a pituitary macroadenoma 3 months ago. Before surgery she had a bitemporal hemianopia. Her vision feels better. Her endocrinologist wants to document precisely how much of the field defect has recovered.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Formal perimetry maps the visual field defect precisely and is used to monitor recovery.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: document precisely how much of the field defect has recovered
steps.x: Precise mapping of the field = perimetry.

elim: Confrontation is a screening test and too crude to map recovery precisely.
CT does not measure the visual field.
Fundoscopy shows the discs but does not map the field.
Acuity measures central vision only.

steps.x: Answer C: Formal visual field testing (perimetry). Map or monitor a field defect with formal perimetry.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has 3 months of headaches and episodes of a strange smell followed by confusion. Perimetry shows a left superior quadrantanopia. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to characterise the underlying lesion?
questions.e: MRI brain is the gold-standard imaging for characterising the lesion causing a visual field defect, here a right temporal lesion.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to characterise the underlying lesion?
A field defect plus temporal lobe seizures needs the lesion imaged in detail.

elim: EEG supports seizures but does not show the lesion.
LP is not the test for a focal structural lesion and may be unsafe.
OCT images the retina, not the temporal lobe.
X-ray does not show brain lesions.

steps.x: Answer C: MRI brain. MRI brain is gold standard for the lesion behind a field defect.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has had a sudden right homonymous hemianopia for 1 hour. She takes no anticoagulants. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 92 bpm irregular, BP 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L. She is assessed by the stroke team.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Sudden homonymous hemianopia is an emergency: follow the stroke pathway, with immediate non-contrast CT to exclude haemorrhage before treatment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

clues: sudden right homonymous hemianopia for 1 hour
steps.x: Suspected acute stroke within the treatment window needs urgent CT first.

elim: This is part of later stroke work-up, not the first test.
This is a later investigation for a cardiac source.
Mapping the field must not delay emergency stroke imaging.
LP is not part of acute stroke assessment.

steps.x: Answer E: Non-contrast CT head. Acute stroke pathway: urgent non-contrast CT head.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl has headaches, poor growth and has started waking at night to drink water. Visual fields show a bitemporal hemianopia worse in the lower quadrants. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: MRI brain is the gold standard for characterising the lesion; here a craniopharyngioma pressing on the chiasm from above, with diabetes insipidus.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

clues: bitemporal hemianopia worse in the lower quadrants
steps.x: Lower bitemporal loss with polyuria in a child = suprasellar lesion; image it.

elim: The lesion is intracranial.
Fundoscopy does not show the lesion.
X-ray may show calcification but cannot characterise the lesion.
This confirms diabetes insipidus but does not show the cause of the field defect.

steps.x: Answer C: MRI brain. Characterise the lesion with MRI brain.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has acromegaly with a bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 2 cm pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm from below. His IGF-1 is raised. He is fit for surgery. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: A pituitary adenoma causing bitemporal hemianopia is treated with trans-sphenoidal surgery.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?

clues: pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm
steps.x: Chiasmal compression by a pituitary adenoma: remove it.

elim: The pituitary is approached through the sphenoid sinus, not the occiput.
Thrombolysis is for ischaemic stroke.
His vision is threatened; the tumour needs treating.
This is not first-line for a pituitary adenoma.

steps.x: Answer D: Trans-sphenoidal surgery. Pituitary adenoma with field loss = trans-sphenoidal surgery.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has a right inferior quadrantanopia. MRI shows a well-circumscribed 3 cm meningioma pressing on the left parietal lobe. She is otherwise well and fit for surgery. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Treat the underlying condition: tumours other than pituitary adenomas causing field defects are treated surgically.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: meningioma pressing on the left parietal lobe
steps.x: The tumour is the cause; removing it is the treatment.

elim: Aspirin is for ischaemic stroke.
These do not treat the underlying tumour.
This is for acute ischaemic stroke.
This approach is for pituitary tumours, not a parietal meningioma.

steps.x: Answer B: Neurosurgical resection of the tumour. Other tumours causing field defects: surgery.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man noticed loss of the left half of his vision 26 hours ago and attends today. CT head shows a right occipital infarct with no haemorrhage. He is in sinus rhythm. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 158/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: No treatment, as it is only a visual defect
questions.e: A field defect from stroke is managed along the standard stroke pathway: outside the thrombolysis window, give aspirin 300 mg.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

clues: right occipital infarct with no haemorrhage
steps.x: Ischaemic stroke too late for thrombolysis: antiplatelet.

elim: He is in sinus rhythm, so there is no indication for anticoagulation.
He is outside the 4.5 hour thrombolysis window.
This is an ischaemic stroke and needs standard stroke management.
This treats pituitary adenomas.

steps.x: Answer A: Aspirin 300 mg daily. Stroke-related field defect: follow the stroke pathway.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has a permanent left homonymous hemianopia 4 months after a stroke. She keeps missing food on the left of her plate, bumps into things and is anxious about going out. Her secondary prevention is optimised. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to improve her daily function?
o: Referral for visual rehabilitation and scanning training
questions.e: Poorly managed field defects reduce quality of life; rehabilitation teaches compensatory scanning to the blind side.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step to improve her daily function?

clues: missing food on the left of her plate
steps.x: The defect is permanent, so the aim is to reduce its impact on quality of life.

elim: Her acuity problem is not the issue; the field loss is cortical.
Repeat imaging will not improve function.
Betahistine is for Ménière's disease.
This treats pituitary tumours.

steps.x: Answer B: Referral for visual rehabilitation and scanning training. Permanent field defect: rehabilitation to protect quality of life.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man phones NHS 111. Thirty minutes ago he suddenly lost the left half of his vision in both eyes and feels off balance. He has hypertension and smokes. He asks whether he can wait to see his optician tomorrow.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Start aspirin and wait to see if it improves
questions.e: Sudden-onset homonymous hemianopia is a concern for posterior circulation stroke and is an emergency: follow the stroke pathway.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice?

clues: suddenly lost the left half of his vision in both eyes
steps.x: Sudden homonymous loss with imbalance = possible posterior stroke within the treatment window.

elim: Delay could miss the window for stroke treatment.
This is a neurological emergency, not an eye problem for the optician.
Aspirin should not be given before imaging excludes haemorrhage.
This ignores a possible stroke.

steps.x: Answer B: Call 999 for emergency stroke assessment. Sudden homonymous hemianopia: emergency stroke pathway.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman with a known non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma has noticed over 2 weeks that her bitemporal field loss is spreading. Perimetry confirms marked deterioration since last month. MRI shows the tumour has enlarged and is pressing hard on the chiasm. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure and repeat perimetry in 12 months
questions.e: Untreated or progressive chiasmal compression risks permanent vision loss; trans-sphenoidal surgery decompresses the chiasm.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Progressive loss means the window to save vision is closing.

elim: This is for ischaemic stroke.
Steroids do not decompress the chiasm.
Progressive compression risks permanent vision loss.
This is not used for a pituitary adenoma threatening vision.

steps.x: Answer D: Urgent trans-sphenoidal surgery. Progressive pituitary compression: urgent trans-sphenoidal surgery.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has a small lesion just behind the optic tract on the left, before the fibres fan out into the optic radiations. A student is tracing the visual pathway from the retina to the cortex.
questions.q: Which structure is most likely affected?
questions.e: The visual pathway runs retina, optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiations, then visual (occipital) cortex.

steps.x: The question asks: Which structure is most likely affected?

clues: before the fibres fan out into the optic radiations
steps.x: The relay between tract and radiations is the thalamic lateral geniculate nucleus.

elim: This is part of the auditory pathway.
This is the thalamic relay for hearing.
The chiasm lies in front of the optic tract.
This lies at the end of the optic radiations in the occipital lobe.

steps.x: Answer B: Lateral geniculate nucleus. Tract to LGN to radiations to occipital cortex.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has a pituitary adenoma pressing on the middle of the optic chiasm. She has lost the temporal half of the visual field in each eye. A student asks which retinal fibres are damaged.
questions.q: Which fibres are most likely damaged?
o: Fibres from the macula of one eye only
Nasal retinal fibres from both eyes
Temporal retinal fibres from both eyes
Temporal retinal fibres from one eye
questions.e: Nasal retinal fibres carry temporal visual field information and cross at the chiasm; a chiasmal lesion damages those from both eyes, giving bitemporal loss.

steps.x: The question asks: Which fibres are most likely damaged?

clues: temporal half of the visual field in each eye
steps.x: The crossing fibres at the chiasm are nasal fibres, which see the temporal fields.

elim: This would cause a central scotoma in one eye.
Meyer's loop is in the temporal lobe and causes a superior quadrantanopia.
Temporal fibres stay uncrossed and carry the nasal fields.
This would cause a nasal defect in one eye.

steps.x: Answer C: Nasal retinal fibres from both eyes. Chiasm lesion = both nasal retinas = bitemporal hemianopia.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has a right optic tract lesion and a left homonymous hemianopia. A student asks why a lesion on one side of the brain affects the vision of both eyes, unlike his previous optic nerve problem.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Behind the chiasm, fibres from the same half of both retinas travel together
Each optic tract carries fibres from one eye only
Nasal fibres stop crossing after the chiasm
The optic tracts receive blood from the macula
The two optic nerves join in the occipital cortex
questions.e: Posterior to the chiasm, fibres from the same side of both eyes travel together, so lesions cause homonymous field defects in both eyes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation?

clues: affects the vision of both eyes
steps.x: After the chiasm each tract carries one half of the visual world from both eyes.

elim: Each tract carries fibres from both eyes.
Nasal fibres have already crossed at the chiasm.
Blood supply does not explain the homonymous pattern.
The nerves meet at the chiasm, not the cortex.

steps.x: Answer A: Behind the chiasm, fibres from the same half of both retinas travel together. Post-chiasmal lesions = homonymous defects.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a left parietal lobe infarct. Perimetry shows a right inferior quadrantanopia. A student asks why the defect is in the lower rather than the upper part of the field.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Meyer's loop in the parietal lobe carries the inferior field
The macula is supplied by two arteries
The optic chiasm carries only lower field fibres
The parietal lobe receives only nasal retinal fibres
The superior optic radiation in the parietal lobe carries the inferior visual field
questions.e: The superior optic radiation passes through the parietal lobe and carries the inferior visual field; Meyer's loop (temporal) carries the superior field.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation?

clues: lower rather than the upper part of the field
steps.x: PITS: Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior; the upper radiations see the lower world.

elim: Meyer's loop runs in the temporal lobe and carries the superior field.
Dual supply explains macular sparing, not quadrant site.
The chiasm carries fibres from all of the temporal fields.
Radiations carry fibres from both eyes.

steps.x: Answer E: The superior optic radiation in the parietal lobe carries the inferior visual field. Parietal lesion hits the superior radiation = inferior quadrantanopia.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man has a left homonymous hemianopia after a right occipital infarct. Surprisingly, his central vision and reading are preserved. A student asks why.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the preserved central vision?
o: Macular fibres cross twice at the chiasm
Macular fibres travel in Meyer's loop
The macula is represented only in the frontal lobe
The occipital pole has a dual blood supply from the posterior and middle cerebral arteries
questions.e: The occipital pole (macula) has a dual blood supply from the posterior cerebral artery and MCA collaterals, so macular vision is often spared in occipital infarcts.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for the preserved central vision?

clues: central vision and reading are preserved
steps.x: Macular sparing in occipital infarcts reflects the extra MCA supply to the occipital pole.

elim: Macular fibres do not cross twice.
Meyer's loop carries the superior field, not the macula.
The macula is represented at the occipital pole.
Tract involvement is not the explanation; the cortex blood supply is.

steps.x: Answer D: The occipital pole has a dual blood supply from the posterior and middle cerebral arteries. Macular sparing = dual blood supply of the occipital pole.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with atrial fibrillation suddenly develops a right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. She has no weakness, sensory loss or speech disturbance.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.e: The left posterior cerebral artery supplies the left visual (occipital) cortex; MCA collaterals to the occipital pole spare the macula.

steps.x: The question asks: Which artery is most likely occluded?

clues: right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
no weakness, sensory loss or speech disturbance
steps.x: Isolated homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing = contralateral occipital cortex, PCA territory.

elim: ACA occlusion causes contralateral leg weakness.
MCA occlusion causes weakness and aphasia, and the macula would not be spared.
This causes monocular loss in the right eye.
A right PCA infarct causes a left homonymous hemianopia.

steps.x: Answer C: Left posterior cerebral artery. Isolated macular-sparing hemianopia = contralateral PCA infarct.
